articles.title: The ASEAN-India Trade Agreement and Its Discontents - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: The ASEAN-India Trade Agreement and Its Discontents  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
Even as India has embraced a renewed fervor for free trade agreements, one trade deal remains disfavored in Indian memory. The 2009 ASEAN-India Goods in Trade Agreement (AITIGA) is one of the oldest trade agreements signed by post-liberalization India as well as one of its most controversial. Atypically for an establishment that prefers to settle diplomatic disputes behind the scenes, Indian diplomats and trade officials are publicly trenchant in their criticism of AITIGA.
An oft-repeated narrative has emerged around the agreement: in the early 2000s, inexperienced Indian negotiators walked into an asymmetric deal, opening up their markets while getting little in return. Consequently, India’s trade deficit with ASEAN ballooned. Moreover, China exploited the AITIGA to route its goods into India through Southeast Asia.
This narrative stems from misremembering history. Rather than a powerful tool for ASEAN and China to penetrate the Indian market, the AITIGA is, in fact, a shallow and weak instrument. Moreover, it is shallow precisely because India preferred it that way. By repeatedly telling itself an alternative story, New Delhi has developed irrational fears over economic cooperation with Southeast Asia and injected unnecessary acrimony in the relationship. The myth of AITIGA as a bad deal is costing India diplomatically.
India started running a trade deficit with ASEAN in 1996, 13 years before the AITIGA was signed. The deficit stemmed from Southeast Asia’s shift from agrarian to manufacturing-led economies. The currency devaluations triggered by the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis further boosted the deficit. While the absolute figure of the trade deficit has ballooned over the last three decades, the India-ASEAN imports-to-exports ratio remains broadly similar to what it was in the 1990s.
After the 1997 crisis, ASEAN was looking to economically integrate itself with its East Asian neighbors. In the early 2000s, it began pursuing ASEAN+1 FTAs with its six immediate neighbors: China, India, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand. India had been excluded from the first wave of post-1997 regional integration – the ASEAN Plus Three, Asian Bond Markets Initiative, and Chiang Mai Initiative for currency swap. Eager not to miss out on another wave of regional integration, India agreed to negotiate the FTA.
Contrary to the myth, Indian officials were tough negotiators. After all, India had decades of experience negotiating economic deals in the GATT, WTO, and elsewhere. The negotiations were tortuous and took much longer than the other ASEAN+1 FTAs.
Moreover, there was a mismatch of approach. On the one hand, eager to gain access to the Indian market, ASEAN wanted to widen the FTA’s scope. On the other hand, India looked to protect its domestic industry by limiting the scope of the agreement. Indian businesses were lukewarm about seeking out greater market access in Southeast Asia.
India’s tough negotiating ensured that the AITIGA was the shallowest of the ASEAN+1 FTAs. Whereas all other agreements committed parties to tariff elimination coverage of more than 90 percent, the AITIGA’s promised coverage hovered around 79 percent. ASEAN mirrored India’s reluctance to open its markets. For instance, Indian critics of the AITIGA often point to the fact that Indonesia promised only 48.7 percent tariff elimination coverage to India. Notably, Indonesia offered above 91 percent coverage to all other ASEAN+1 partners, including Australia, with which it ran a trade deficit at the time.
AITIGA also ended up with the most stringent Rules of Origin among all the ASEAN+1 FTAs. It is the only agreement that demands dual compliance (35 percent local content and change in tariff subheading) for goods to qualify for preferential treatment. Its complex compliance rules and lower scope resulted in exporters avoiding using the AITIGA.
In AITIGA, India got what it wanted – an agreement that signaled India’s commitment to its Look East policy without exposing its domestic industry to excessive international competition. While economists may argue over whether Indian protectionism is good economic policy, the debate is irrelevant from a diplomatic standpoint. For whatever reasons, Indian economic managers prefer shielding the Indian market. The AITIGA was a natural outcome of such preference.
However, to then construct a narrative of the agreement as a bad deal in which India got duped is diplomatically damaging. To begin with, it erodes India’s credibility in the region as a reliable and competent partner. India began criticizing the AITIGA almost as soon as it was signed. The two sides agreed to open a review of the agreement in 2015 but still haven’t concluded it. Such long-drawn, dangling processes chip away at India’s image.
AITIGA’s beleaguered state becomes a particularly bad look when contrasted with other ASEAN+1 FTAs, especially the one with China. Beijing began negotiating its FTA with ASEAN around the same time as New Delhi. However, it not only concluded the negotiations fairly quickly, but China and ASEAN have since upgraded the agreement twice. Today, the ASEAN-China FTA is a powerful instrument that deals with a range of issues from digital trade to green technology.
The narrative of AITIGA as a loss for India has made New Delhi a less confident economic actor in Southeast Asia. The resultant hesitation has been evident in India’s exit from the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership as well as its reluctance to conclude bilateral FTAs with Southeast Asian countries such as Thailand and Indonesia. Today, even as India seeks out FTAs in the Middle East and Europe, it is too unsure of itself to look for a trade deal in Southeast Asia.
Tellingly, the acrimony over AITIGA has spilled over into other aspects of ASEAN-India economic cooperation, even the ones which are in India’s interests. For instance, the 2014 ASEAN-India Trade in Services Agreement needs urgent upgradation to account for all the advancements in the digital economy. Given that India enjoys a services surplus with Southeast Asia, New Delhi should be eagerly driving the process. However, so far the two sides have not even begun discussing the issue.
The self-created myths around AITIGA have cast a shadow on India’s Look/Act East policy. New Delhi needs to shed them to become a more confident, credible and engaged actor in the region.

articles.title: India-EU FTA to benefit Netherlands as trade, investment ties expand: Indian envoy to Netherlands Tuhin - India's News.Net

articles.full_text:
By Sahil Pandey
Hague [Netherlands], October 27 (ANI): India's Ambassador to the Netherlands, Kumar Tuhin, has said the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) will significantly benefit the Netherlands by expanding trade and investment flows, highlighting the country's position as a key European economic and logistics hub.
Speaking to ANI, Tuhin said the visit of Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal to the Netherlands was successful in advancing economic cooperation following the elevation of India-Netherlands ties to a strategic partnership during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit a few months ago.
"The visit of Union Commerce and Industry Minister to the Netherlands was very successful, especially because it came in the backdrop of the visit of Prime Minister Modi a few months ago and the upgrading of our relations to a strategic partnership," Tuhin said.
He said the visit aimed to strengthen economic, commercial and business relations, while conveying to Dutch leadership and industry representatives India's economic growth trajectory and the structural complementarities between the two countries.
"What this visit did was to convey to the Dutch leadership and industry captains was how we are preparing to strengthen the economic and trade aspect of our relationship and to prepare those elements of the strategic partnership," the ambassador said.
Emphasising the importance of high-level engagement, Tuhin said presenting India's economic outlook and growth potential to Dutch stakeholders would help underline the opportunities arising from the complementary strengths of the two economies.
On the India-EU FTA, the ambassador said the Netherlands was well-positioned to benefit as economic engagement between India and the European Union expands.
'Even now, India and Netherlands has very strong trade and investment ties. Netherlands is India's second largest trading partner in the EU. Also, this is the fourth largest investment destination for the country,' he said.
Tuhin pointed to the Netherlands' strategic advantages, including Rotterdam's role as a major European port and Eindhoven's prominence as a technology and innovation hub, alongside Amsterdam and other economic centres.
'So, as India-EU-FTA comes into play and the overall engagement with the EU expands and overall volume of trade investment expands, Netherlands will be a very beneficiary,' he said, adding that the potential benefits of the agreement were also highlighted during Goyal's interactions with Dutch leadership.
The ambassador's remarks come amid India's efforts to deepen economic engagement with European partners and leverage the proposed India-EU trade agreement to expand market access, investment and technological cooperation.
India and the Netherlands have been seeking to build on their strategic partnership through closer business engagement and stronger economic ties, with the India-EU FTA expected to provide further momentum to bilateral trade and investment. (ANI)

articles.title: India Would Become Major Exporter To China, ASEAN Markets In Coming Years: Piyush Goyal - Free Press Journal
articles.summary: India Would Become Major Exporter To China, ASEAN Markets In Coming Years: Piyush Goyal  Free Press Journal
articles.full_text:
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has expressed confidence that India could emerge as a major exporter of goods and services to China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in the coming years.
Speaking to reporters during a two-day official visit, Goyal said India remained committed to promoting open, fair and reciprocal trade with international partners.
He also referred to discussions with his Chinese counterpart in Yaounde, Cameroon, and New Delhi, highlighting efforts to strengthen economic engagement between the two countries.
India Seeks Greater Market Access In China, ASEAN
Goyal said India was working to secure improved access for its products and services in overseas markets through reciprocal trade arrangements.
He acknowledged China's role in supplying intermediate goods and raw materials required by Indian industries.
However, he emphasised that concerns over unfair pricing or trade practices would be addressed through established legal procedures.
The minister maintained that India welcomed international suppliers capable of meeting its expanding domestic requirements.
He expressed hope that Indian businesses would substantially increase exports to China and Southeast Asian economies.
ASEAN includes Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Goyal's remarks followed his Oct 14 statement that India was working towards rebuilding relations with China, although the process remained incomplete.
India-China Relations Improve After Border Tensions
Bilateral ties had deteriorated sharply following the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and the prolonged military standoff in eastern Ladakh.
However, both countries have undertaken diplomatic measures in recent months to improve relations.
The rapprochement gained momentum after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024, following the resolution of the military face-off.
The leaders subsequently met on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi in September 2026.

articles.title: "Farmers more important than anyone...": Karnataka CM Shivakumar says sugarcane price talks near agreement - India's News.Net
articles.summary: "Farmers more important than anyone...": Karnataka CM Shivakumar says sugarcane price talks near agreement  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
Belagavi (Karnataka) [India], October 27 (ANI): Karnataka DK Shivakumar on Tuesday said the state government and sugarcane farmers had moved close to an agreement following extensive discussions involving farmer leaders, legislators, ministers, sugar factory representatives and government officials over the sugarcane pricing issue.
Addressing the media in Belagavi, Shivakumar said the discussions began at 11 am and continued until 12.30 am, with representatives from across the state participating in the talks. He said around 70 MLAs and MPs, nine ministers and officials from the Finance Department and other departments were also involved in the discussions.
"All my ministerial colleagues and farmer leaders have been engaged in lengthy discussions since 11 a.m. this morning, and the discussions continued until 12:30 a.m. tonight. Farm leaders from every corner of the state, from all districts, had come. Along with them, about 70 MLAs, MPs, about 9 Ministers and all officers from the Finance Department and others have come and held detailed discussions," Shivakumar said.
He said sugar factories had agreed to abide by the rate fixed following the discussions and make the subsequent payments to farmers accordingly. Emphasising the government's position, he said the welfare and survival of farmers remained its priority.
'Whatever rate is fixed, whatever is to be given after that fixation, our factories have agreed to it. For the government, farmers are more important than anyone; they must survive - that is the decision. So we all sat and discussed for two days. They have asked for two more days; they have come close to an agreement. Today we have come to a happy ending. In two more days they themselves will discuss and come to a decision,' he said.
Shivakumar added that the discussions had brought the stakeholders close to a resolution, with farmers and sugar factory representatives expected to meet again within two days to reach a decision.
He further stated that the next meeting could take place in Belagavi or Bengaluru, depending on their convenience and assured farmers of the government's continued support.
'We have come very close to resolving this as soon as possible. In two more days, the factories and farmers will sit together and take a decision - whether in Belagavi or in Bengaluru, at their convenience. From our side, whatever encouragement has to be given to farmers, we will stand in support of them. I am committed to go and talk to the Central Government at any time if needed,' he added.
On the ongoing sugarcane farmers' protest, the Chief Minister said the state government had already held discussions with sugar factories and would now consult its officials before taking further steps. He stressed that the Centre's involvement was necessary to resolve the pricing issue, as the factories would not agree to a floor price without the sugar price being fixed.
'We have discussed with the factories. Now we have to discuss with our officers. Now, without taking the Central Government into confidence, we cannot do anything. Without the sugar price being fixed, they will not cooperate on the floor price. I am requesting first: Farmers, you should allow the harvesting of sugarcane. We will call some leaders, the factory owners and also talk to the Central Government, convince their committee, and we will take a decision immediately. I have requested them to cooperate with this. I request that you allow farmers to harvest your crop,' he said.
Reiterating the state government's support for the farmers, Shivakumar questioned the need for continued protests and assured them that the government was on their side. He also said he had written to the Prime Minister regarding the matter.
'Why protest? We are on your side; we are on the farmers' side. I have written to the Prime Minister also,' he said.
Shivakumar reiterated that the government would continue engaging with farmers, sugar factory owners and the Central Government to decide on the sugarcane price issue, while extending the necessary support to farmers. (ANI)

Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned that any attempt to exclude Russia from the global gas market would have serious consequences, while signalling potential cooperation with US partners in the resource-rich Arctic.
Speaking at a summit of gas-exporting countries in Moscow on Tuesday, Putin said Russia remained open to cooperation in the gas sector and was exploring the possibility of working with US partners.
He also cautioned against placing excessive emphasis on the green agenda, arguing that energy policy should account for the need to maintain reliable supplies.
Putin's remarks come as Russia seeks to protect its position in global energy markets and explore new opportunities for cooperation amid geopolitical tensions.

articles.title: After Canada fires back with retaliatory tariffs, Trump and Carney move to ease trade war in 2 sectors as South Africa braces for U.S. duty slap - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: After Canada fires back with retaliatory tariffs, Trump and Carney move to ease trade war in 2 sectors as South Africa braces for U.S. duty slap  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Washington and Ottawa are negotiating to reduce U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and automotive imports to ease recent trade tensions.
- Talks focus on targeted relief from Section 232 duties, which now impose up to 50% levies on Canadian steel and 25% on vehicles.
- Canada had previously imposed heavy retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods, especially targeting politically sensitive areas.
- Meanwhile, South Africa may lose its preferential trade access to the U.S. under AGOA, risking major economic impact, especially in automotive manufacturing.
According to sources cited by Reuters, government officials are actively discussing targeted relief from Section 232 duties, which currently include levies of up to 50% on Canadian steel and 25% on motor vehicles.
The prospective agreement marks a shift toward diplomacy after months of escalating trade measures between the neighboring economies.
The U.S. and Canada seek common ground on steel and auto tariffs
High-level negotiations between Washington and Ottawa have intensified as both governments attempt to reach a narrowed agreement ahead of upcoming U.S. midterm elections.
U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Canadian Minister Dominic LeBlanc have maintained regular contact to negotiate duty relief.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed a "slight intensification" in bilateral talks, stating, "To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the US is coming closer to our position," according to Reuters.
As reported by Business Insider Africa in August, Carney had previously pledged that Ottawa would respond to American trade penalties "dollar for dollar".
Before the current negotiations gained momentum, Canada enacted heavy retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on roughly 700 American products, covering approximately $20 billion in annual imports.
Canadian Trade Minister Mélanie Joly explained in reports published by Business Insider Africa that Ottawa specifically selected goods from U.S. states supporting President Donald Trump to maximize political impact.
Joly noted that while Canadian officials held "a lot of good cards," they elected not to deploy their most severe economic measures immediately.
South Africa faces potential trade fallout as U.S. AGOA decision looms
While North American partners negotiate duty relief, South Africa is bracing for a potential trade breakup with the United States as executive approval for its continued access under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) remains uncertain.
Although the U.S. Congress voted to extend South Africa's duty-free market access through 2028, final authorization rests with President Donald Trump amid diplomatic tensions over land reform and discrimination claims.
Addressing the nation, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa warned citizens about the pending decision, stating, "Congress has decided that we should be kept in AGOA. What now remains is the executive," while adding, "if we ever have a choice, we are not the first and only country to be taken out of AGOA. And I believe we will not be the last."
The loss of preferential market access threatens severe consequences for South Africa's economy, particularly its automotive manufacturing sector.
According to data from the national automobile manufacturing body Naamsa cited by Business Insider Africa, roughly 86,000 direct manufacturing jobs and over 125,000 total positions rely directly on the trade agreement.
President Ramaphosa called losing duty-free trade access "devastating," but he urged South Africans to stay resilient.
According to Business Insider Africa, he stated, "I need, as president, to prepare us if it ever happens. So we should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world."

articles.title: India-Chile FTA Talks 'Quite Ripe' For Conclusion, Canada Negotiations Making Progress: Goyal - Outlook India
articles.summary: India-Chile FTA Talks 'Quite Ripe' For Conclusion, Canada Negotiations Making Progress: Goyal  Outlook India
articles.full_text:
- Chile FTA talks are near completion; Canada negotiations progress steadily.
- SACU discussions opened while Mexico seeks an early-harvest deal.
- India created trade SOPs to guide future negotiators.
India is negotiating free trade agreements (FTAs) with several countries and groups, with talks with Chile "quite ripe" for conclusion and negotiations with Canada making good progress, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said.
He said that negotiations with the South Africa-led SACU (Southern African Customs Union) group have started.
Negotiations With Latin America And SACU
The two have inked terms of reference (ToR) to formally start negotiations towards a preferential trade agreement in August. The five members of SACU are Botswana, Eswatini (formerly Swaziland), Lesotho, Namibia and South Africa.
He was here for a two-day official visit. Talking about other pacts, he said Mexico is "very" keen to have an early harvest trade agreement.
Expanding Scope Across Global Blocs
He expressed hope that the continuity of the government in Brazil following the election would help speed up negotiations to expand the Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) with the Mercosur bloc.
Mercosur is a trade bloc in South America comprising Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Uruguay, and Paraguay. The India-Mercosur PTA came into effect on June 1, 2009. The agreement provides preferential tariff concessions on 450 tariff lines or product categories by India and 452 tariff lines by the Mercosur side. Now both sides are looking to expand the scope of the pact.
He added that negotiations with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Israel for "obvious" reasons are slow due to the West Asia crisis, and it may take some time.
"Though we are ready to speed up negotiations," he said.
The GCC comprises Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and was established in 1981 as a political, economic and security grouping. India already has a trade pact with the UAE and Oman.
"Eurasia FTA is only about goods; it doesn't include services. Hence, we are still assessing the benefits of entering into that agreement," Goyal said.
India and the five-nation grouping, the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), on August 20 last year, inked the terms of reference to formally start talks for the agreement. The first round of negotiations was held in November 2025.
"Many other countries are talking to us. Ecuador (a South American nation) wants to do an FTA. Egypt has invited us to Egypt to discuss potentially how we can work more. Other African countries have been approaching us, either to have an FTA with all of Africa, or with the African Union or the sectoral FTA's," he said.
In the trade pact with the US, he said India will have a comparative advantage over other countries and get preferential access.
India and the US, in February , announced finalization of the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement (BTA). However, changes in the tariff landscape in the US have led to further negotiations on the pact.
Institutionalizing Standard Operating Trade Manuals
When asked about capacity building for conducting these negotiations, the minister said Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been very focused on ensuring that the negotiations, along with all the learnings and efforts involved, do not become a one-time affair.
"And therefore, in the last three years or so, we've prepared proper manuals, which are a guide like a standard operating procedure (SOP) towards proper and organised FTA negotiations," he said, adding, "Every FTA that we enter into, we prepare a lot of documentation for future reference and to help guide officers in the future, because people keep changing."
The minister is here on a two-day official visit. He is accompanying a business delegation.

articles.title: Drug Manufacturing Plant Setup Cost in India - IMARC Group
articles.summary: Drug Manufacturing Plant Setup Cost in India  IMARC Group
articles.full_text:
Generic formulations are finished medicines, such as tablets and capsules, that contain the same active ingredient, strength, and effect as an original brand once its patent expires. Oral solid dosage forms make up the largest share of medicines taken worldwide, and India supplies a large part of the world's generics, ranking third globally by volume. India's domestic pharmaceutical market is about USD 60 billion and is projected to reach USD 130 billion by 2030, while exports reached USD 30.5 billion in FY2025, with the US taking about a third. A large chronic disease burden, growing health insurance coverage, government procurement, and export demand make Drug Manufacturing Plant Setup in India a strong opportunity for pharma entrepreneurs and healthcare investors.
Investment depends mainly on capacity, the range of dosage forms, the level of automation, cleanroom and HVAC standards, quality control laboratories, and whether the plant targets domestic markets under revised Schedule M or regulated markets such as the US and Europe. The Drug Manufacturing Plant Cost ranges from about INR 20–35 crore for a compact oral solid unit of 300 to 500 million tablets a year to INR 60–100 crore for a WHO-GMP plant of about 1 billion tablets and 300 million capsules a year, and INR 250–450 crore for a large facility of 3 to 5 billion units built to US FDA and EU standards. Raw materials, led by active ingredients, make up 40 to 50% of operating cost and utilities 20 to 25%. IMARC estimates a gross margin of 55 to 65% and a net margin of 25 to 35% for a well-run plant, though contract manufacturers usually earn less than branded and export-focused companies.
This guide is written for investors exploring how to start a Drug manufacturing plant in India. It focuses on a WHO-GMP oral solid dosage plant of about 1 billion tablets and 300 million capsules a year, producing generic tablets, capsules, and sachets for branded generic marketers, contract customers, government tenders, and semi-regulated export markets, and also explains compact units and regulated-market facilities. It covers products and markets, the demand outlook, the production process flow, machinery and raw materials, location and infrastructure, a detailed cost and financial breakdown, licensing and GMP, and how a DPR and financial model turn all of this into a bankable plan.

The snapshot shows a large, fast-growing domestic market and a strong export base, with India among the world's leading suppliers of generic medicines. Active ingredients dominate material costs, and much of India's supply of key ingredients still comes from China, so sourcing and quality matter greatly. Compliance with revised Schedule M is now mandatory for all makers, so building to GMP standards from the start is essential. The wide investment range reflects a real choice between a compact domestic unit, a WHO-GMP plant, and a regulated-market facility.
Indicative Project Cost in India (2026)
| Parameter | Value | 
|---|---|
| Product Range | Tablets, capsules, coated, sachets | 
| Plant Capacity | 300 Million – 5 Billion Units Per Year | 
| Total Project Investment | INR 20–35 Crore (compact unit) to 250–450 Crore (regulated plant) | 
| Payback Period | 3 – 5 Years | 
| Net Profit Margin | 25 – 35% | 
| IRR | 20 – 28% | 
| Preferred States | Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh | 
| Key Requirement | Drug license, Schedule M, product dossiers | 
These ranges provide a realistic frame for early planning, but actual returns depend on active ingredient prices, many of which still rely on Chinese supply, the product portfolio and its price controls, the speed of product licenses and export registrations, competition from thousands of formulators, price caps under drug price control rules, and the cost of meeting GMP inspections. A site-specific Drug Feasibility Report narrows each of these assumptions to your chosen products, capacity, location, and markets.
Table of Contents
A formulation plant does not make the active ingredient itself; it buys the active pharmaceutical ingredient, or API, and combines it with excipients such as fillers, binders, disintegrants, and lubricants, then converts the mixture into tablets, capsules, or powders of exact strength. Each batch must contain the right amount of active ingredient, dissolve as intended in the body, stay stable through its shelf life, and be free of contamination. Content uniformity, dissolution, impurities, hardness and friability, stability, and complete batch documentation decide quality, and all are governed by pharmacopoeia standards and GMP rules.
Commercially, formulations are sold to branded generic marketers that sell to doctors and pharmacies, through contract and loan license manufacturing for other companies, to central and state government tenders and Jan Aushadhi stores, to hospitals, and to export buyers in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and, with approvals, the US and Europe. A Drug Manufacturing Plant can serve all these channels by building a broad, registered portfolio. Buyers value consistent quality, regulatory compliance, reliable delivery, documentation for registrations, and competitive prices.
The Main Dosage Forms and Applications
Choosing the product mix is the most important commercial decision, because it determines equipment, cleanroom design, and customers:
| Dosage Form | Description | Key Property | Primary Demand | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Uncoated Tablets | Compressed granules | Low cost | Pain, infections | 
| Film-Coated Tablets | Polymer coat | Taste, stability | Chronic therapies | 
| Modified-Release | Controlled release | Once-daily dosing | Diabetes, heart | 
| Hard Capsules | Powder or pellets | Easy to swallow | Antibiotics, PPIs | 
| Dispersible Tablets | Dissolve in water | For children | Paediatric care | 
| Powders & Sachets | ORS, dry syrups | Easy dosing | Children, rehydration | 
These choices shape the whole plant. Uncoated and coated tablets and capsules for common acute and chronic therapies are the volume products, while modified-release and specialty forms need extra equipment, development skills, and stability studies, but earn better margins. Products such as hormones, cytotoxics, and penicillins need dedicated, segregated facilities. Most new entrants start with general tablets and capsules for chronic and acute therapies, then add modified-release forms and export registrations as their quality systems mature.
Key Growth Drivers in India and Export Markets
Demand is supported by health needs at home and India's strength as a generic supplier abroad:
India-Specific Market Opportunity
| Segment | Market Context | Manufacturing Role | 
|---|---|---|
| Branded Generics | Large domestic market | Own or partner brands | 
| Contract Makers | Outsourcing growth | Third-party supply | 
| Government Tenders | Jan Aushadhi, states | Bulk generics | 
| Semi-Regulated Exports | Africa, Asia, LatAm | WHO-GMP products | 
The strongest opportunity for new entrants lies in contract manufacturing for India's many marketing companies, in government and Jan Aushadhi supply, and in exports to semi-regulated markets once WHO-GMP certification and product registrations are in place. Producers that combine reliable API sourcing, a strong quality system, and a well-chosen product portfolio will be best placed to grow.
Understanding the process helps you plan equipment, layout, and where cost and quality are decided. The flow runs from dispensing of raw materials through sifting, dry mixing, wet granulation, drying, milling, blending and lubrication, compression or capsule filling, coating, and inspection and packing, with in-process checks and release testing at every stage. Granulation and blending decide content uniformity, while compression and coating decide dissolution, appearance, and stability.
The Drug Manufacturing Process Flow
The sequence below reflects a wet granulation tablet line. Direct compression products skip granulation and drying, and capsules are filled instead of compressed.
| Unit Operation | Key Activity | 
|---|---|
| Dispensing | Weighing under LAF | 
| Sifting | Remove lumps | 
| Dry Mixing | API and excipients | 
| Wet Granulation | Binder added | 
| Drying | Fluid bed dryer | 
| Milling & Sizing | Uniform granules | 
| Blending | Lubricant added | 
| Compression | Rotary press | 
| Coating | Film coat | 
| Inspection & Packing | Blister, strip, bottle | 
Two factors decide profitability across this flow. The first is right-first-time quality, because a single failed batch wastes costly active ingredients, ties up capacity, and can trigger regulatory action, so validated processes, trained staff, and robust documentation directly protect margins. The second is changeover efficiency, since a generic plant makes many products in small batches, and fast, validated cleaning between products determines how much the plant can produce.
The main raw materials are active pharmaceutical ingredients from domestic or imported suppliers, excipients such as microcrystalline cellulose, lactose, starch, povidone, croscarmellose, and magnesium stearate, coating materials and empty capsule shells, and packaging such as aluminium foil, PVC or PVdC film, bottles, cartons, and leaflets.
| Raw Material | Role in Product | India Sourcing | % of OpEx | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Active Ingredients | Therapeutic effect | Domestic, China | 30–38% | 
| Excipients | Fillers, binders | Domestic suppliers | 4–6% | 
| Coatings & Capsules | Coat, shells | Domestic suppliers | 2–4% | 
| Primary Packaging | Foil, film, bottles | Domes

articles.title: Artisans : Saving Kashmir Economy - Greater Kashmir
articles.summary: Artisans : Saving Kashmir Economy  Greater Kashmir
articles.full_text:
The timing of the National Education Policy 2020 aligned with the country’s broader realization of the fact that it might be experiencing a demographic dividend! 65% of Indian population will remain in the working age category up to 2030. This number will slightly decline to 62%, by 2050. When a country experiences a situation like this, it is faced by several challenges. Broadly, two things can happen. One, the country is able to harness its big working age population as a productive resource, generate and harness its human capital and develop in a speedy manner. Or two, a country misses this bus and is unable to skill and train its population. In both cases, people populating the working-age category graduate to old-age/non-working category in the next two to three decades.
Currently, 1001.7 million Indians fall in the working-age group. Of this, around 10 million are the residents of Jammu and Kashmir. The official unemployment rate of J&K has been calculated at 06.7%. 473000 (and increasing) working age people from J&K are actively looking for work but continue being unemployed. Around 16% workforce of J&K is employed in the government sector. Roughly 04% work in non-government formal sector. Rest 80% are employed in semi-formal or informal sectors respectively. Of these 80%, more than half are self-employed. Casual labors again form a considerable fraction of this very group.
In the last two years, overall college enrollments in J&K have dropped by 26%!
The National Education Policy 2020, came as the central government’s response to the youth bulge of the country! Given the fact that India currently homes the largest population of the world, this populace in essence and spirit needs to be productive. It needs to be healthy, educated, skillful, smart, upskilling and efficient…
The former model of education, where years of education served as a market signal for the hiring entities lost its relevance a while ago. Modern digital economy runs on axioms that are just shaping up and evolving each passing moment. Collective responses to these changes need to be more reflexive, (calculated) spur of the moment and predictive rather than just retrospective!
Accordingly, under the NEP-2020 module, when a student after passing class XII, enters a college or university to earn her degree, she is required to curate a course basket of six different subjects. A major subject in which one intends to build the core specialization. A minor subject, which is as heavy as core but curated in a way that it aids the learning and skilling of the core course.
Then comes the interesting part. Courses including: a multi-disciplinary, an ability enhancement, a skill enhancement and a value-added course need all to be curated simultaneously.
In spirit, an institution is required to curate these options in a manner that a student’s unique capacity is built. At the end of the eighth or tenth semester when the said student leaves the campus, she, in theory, is expected to be all set and ready to enter the contemporary labour market without any hustle or issues. The axiom behind the idea is that the present job market is complex and skill-driven! As such, a well-educated and a well-skilled individual is expected to best capture the contemporary labor market, predominantly through her own capabilities rather than expecting the government to create job for her.
In practice, unfortunately, the institutions are suffering from multiple bottlenecks and issues. Funding is sparce and staff is limited. Contractual hirings are made quite often; for a few months to a maximum of a year. The curators of the course baskets at the institution level are given the job in dark. Capacity building programs, brain-storming, model institution visits, hands-on and learning-by-demonstration; are all missing!
Focusing on the specific context of Jammu and Kashmir, some changes are easy to make and plausible to be carried out.
On the one hand, our traditional professions like hand-carving, aari-work, tilla-work, paper-machie, Namda making, Kashmiri paper making; only to name a few, are almost entering an extinction phase. The artisans specializing in these crafts are either leaving the profession or simply dying without transferring the skills to any apprentices or successors. Low remunerations, non-recognition, lack of policy support and oblivion have slowly and steadily been eating them up!
On the other hand, markets and the global economy are metamorphosizing. The demand for niche products is increasing. The sense of aesthetically pleasant things is developing and appreciation for unique items is growing, leading to an increase in the demand for such goods.
There is a novel but very interesting idea/portfolio under the NEP-2020 mandates known as; Professor of Practice (PoP). A PoP is a person who has deep expertise, working knowledge, practical experience and specialization in a(ny specific) field or skill. The institutions have the option of inviting such people as the PoPs so that direct contributions are made towards a focal capacity building of the young.
A local solution to our local problem of unemployment and skill constraint has as such, simply been lying around!
If the colleges/universities hire senior artisans as Professors of Practice (PoPs) and curate three-to-four-year courses on different crafts, a student can leave with a degree in a mainstream subject like Economics, Business, Physics, Chemistry or Geomatics along with a fully-developed and mastered marketable skill.
Given the fact that a considerably large portion of modern-day sales and purchases are made online, especially through simpler platforms like Instagram and Facebook, each student given the level of creatively and tech-savviness they have, can become a seller online. Steadily, offline and more formal ventures can be developed under the ‘learning by doing’ framework. A big army of productive, creative and well-educated artisans can be curated in less than five years.
As it seems, the most notable of the very few remaining artisans can finally get the long long-awaited recognition. For an example, senior artisans like Ghulam Rasool Ahangar, Mohammad Shafi Weedah, Bilal Ahmad and curator Mohammad Idris among many others can be thought of, while making deliberations of this sort. With an intervention like this, it can be expected that the Kashmiri handicrafts industry might after all be reincarnated.
Multiple backward and forward linkages can eventually be developed. Over the longer run, a circular economy gets set in place. The pressure on tourism and horticulture with this intervention can be expected to decline. The unemployment rate in J&K will slowly but steadily be able to take care of itself.
An artisan after all has all the potential to save the J&K economy, as he has been doing for centuries at a stretch!

articles.title: Understanding Trump's tariff reversals - Peterson Institute for International Economics
articles.summary: Understanding Trump's tariff reversals  Peterson Institute for International Economics
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump has pitched tariffs to address varied US economic and national security concerns, while also generating revenues. And shortly after taking office in early 2025, he ordered a flurry of new tariffs on nearly all countries. But he also quickly eased or abandoned many of them. This process of imposing and reversing tariffs produced four major types of results, in rough chronological order: stabilization of financial markets, concessions from foreign governments, corporate investment pledges, and lower US consumer prices on some items.
The combined economic effects of reversals are unclear at this point, but to get a rough sense of their relative potential importance, we estimated the hypothetical annual tariff revenues the United States would have collected if each initial tariff threat had been implemented for a year. This measure provides a common basis for comparing the scale of tariff threats and the concessions or reversals that followed. By that measure, the biggest tariff threats served as negotiating leverage for foreign economic concessions, as seen in table 1 below.
| Threatened tariffs annualized and tariffs collected before reversal, by effects category |  |  |  |  | 
| Effects category | Collection window (threat date → date reversal announced) | Threatened tariff amount (annualized) | Actual revenue collected by additional tariff (within window) | Basis for estimate | 
| Financial turmoil — April 9 reciprocal tariff pause |  |  |  |  | 
| Liberation Day reciprocal tariffs (55 countries) | Apr 2 – Apr 9, 2025 (rates in effect only on Apr 9) | $262.7B | NA | Paused reciprocal rates on 2024 import values | 
| Subtotal — financial turmoil |  | $262.7B |  |  | 
| Negotiating leverage — tariff de-escalation deals |  |  |  |  | 
| China, reciprocal IEEPA tariff | Apr 9 – May 12, 2025 | $495.7B | $46.0B | 125% was the negotiated reversal, calculated on 2024 import value | 
| UK tariff negotiations (autos, aircraft) | Apr 3 – Jun 16, 2025 | $1.7B | Autos: $210M; aircraft: $130M; total: $0.3B | Sector-specific rate cuts, 2024 import values | 
| EU tariff negotiations (autos) | Apr 3 – Sep 5, 2025 | $6.3B | $2.7B | Sector-specific rate cuts, 2024 import values | 
| Japan tariff negotiations (autos) | Apr 3 – Jul 22, 2025 | $5.2B | $1.6B | Auto rate cut from 27.5% to 15%, 2024 auto imports | 
| South Korea, reciprocal IEEPA tariff | Apr 2 – Oct 29, 2025 | NA | $8.4B | Negotiated reciprocal tariff rate, 2024 import values | 
| Subtotal — negotiating leverage |  | $508.9B | $59.0B |  | 
| Consumer prices — food tariff relief |  |  |  |  | 
| Agricultural products tariff relief | Apr 2 – Nov 14, 2025 | $2.9B | $1.8B | 10% rate eliminated | 
| Beef tariff quota relief | Apr 2 – Aug 26, 2025 | $2.1B | $0.8 B | 26.4% rate eliminated on first 1.2M tons (annually) | 
| Subtotal — consumer prices |  | $5.0B | $2.6B |  | 
| Industrial subsidies — Section 232 relief |  |  |  |  | 
| Industrial subsidies relief (aluminum) | Apr 2 – Oct 9, 2026 | $5.8B | $1.3B | Company-specific Section 232 rate reductions; only aluminum tariffs were collected before reversal | 
| Subtotal — industrial subsidies |  | $5.8B | $1.3B |  | 
| Total estimated annual revenue forgone |  | ~$782.4B | ~$62.9B collected |  | 
| NA = not applicable Note: Japan and South Korea's Liberation Day reciprocal tariff pauses are excluded under negotiating-leverage tariffs as an exact duplicate of their financial turmoil estimates above. Annualized revenue forgone is estimated by multiplying 2024 imports of the affected goods by the reduction in the tariff rate (peak rate minus the rate after the pause or deal). Revenue collected is estimated by dividing 2024 imports of the affected goods by 366 to get a daily import value, as there were 366 days in 2024. That figure is then multiplied by the number of days the additional tariff was in effect and by the difference between the original tariff rate and the peak rate under the collection window. Both figures are static estimates based on 2024 import values and do not account for changes in trade volumes, product exemptions, or the timing of duty payments. |  |  |  |  | 
| Sources: PIIE calculations of United States International Trade Commission, UN Comtrade, US Census, US Bureau of Economic Analysis, Congressional Budget Office, and Federal Register data. |  |  |  |  | 
Financial turmoil
Soon after Trump announced new tariffs on April 2, 2025—which he dubbed "Liberation Day"—he backtracked on some, with the effect of arresting a stock market rout. On April 2, he had ordered a universal baseline 10 percent tariff on nearly all imports to take effect immediately, and he threatened additional "reciprocal" tariffs on individual trading partners to reflect their bilateral merchandise trade surpluses with the United States, to take effect April 9. During the week following that announcement, the S&P 500 plunged more than 12 percent while yields on 10-year Treasury notes spiked about half of 1 percentage point.
On April 9, Trump paused the "reciprocal" tariffs for 90 days (a period that was later extended) but kept the baseline 10 percent tariff. Stock and bond markets rallied. If all the threatened "reciprocal" tariffs had taken full effect, they would have generated annual US tariff revenue of $262.7 billion, assuming US import volumes and prices did not change in response (the same assumption applies to the subsequent calculations below).
Negotiating leverage
Tariffs are often withdrawn or lowered to press for concessions by a trading partner. Threatened tariffs on imports from China are exhibit A in the use of negotiating leverage. On April 9, 2025, after pausing the "reciprocal" tariffs announced on Liberation Day, Trump threatened an additional tariff of 125 percent on imports from China, worth an annualized $495.7 billion. Beijing quickly retaliated. The massive threatened tariffs jeopardized the global economy. Thus, on May 12, 2025, the United States and China agreed to reduce these tariffs for 90 days to 10 percent on the United States and to 30 percent on China but left in place other US tariffs on China.
On Liberation Day, Trump threatened a 27.5 percent "reciprocal" tariff on the United Kingdom. In June 2025, the United States agreed to reduce this tariff to 10 percent on 100,000 auto imports annually. It also agreed to eliminate the baseline 10 percent tariff on civil aircraft and set a future most-favored-nation quota on steel and aluminum components. In turn, the United Kingdom enlarged market access for US meat and ethanol exports. Before they were withdrawn, the threatened US Liberation Day tariffs on UK autos and aircraft amounted to $1.7 billion.[1]
The United States threatened to impose a 20 percent "reciprocal tariff" on the European Union. On July 27, 2025, Trump met European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen at his golf course in Turnberry, Scotland, and agreed on a framework for US-EU trade and investment. He implemented the framework for the United States with a September 2025 executive order. EU implementation is working its way through the EU Parliament. Combined US tariffs on the European Union were capped at 15 percent. In turn, the European Union agreed to eliminate tariffs on US industrial exports; give US seafood and agricultural exports preferential access; procure US energy, artificial intelligence (AI), and semiconductor exports; and invest $600 billion in US projects over three years. Threatened US tariffs on autos before the Turnberry deal amounted to $6.3 billion annualized.
Late in July 2025, the United States and Japan reached a framework agreement, recorded in a September 2025 memorandum of understanding. The 24 percent US Liberation Day tariffs on Japan were generally capped at 15 percent, but separate tariffs of 50 percent on steel, aluminum, and copper remained in place. In turn, Japan agreed to invest $550 billion in US projects, buy 100 Boeing aircraft, increase its rice imports by 75 percent, and buy $8 billion of other US agricultural products. Before the July 2025 deal, threatened tariffs on auto imports from Japan amounted to $5.2 billion annualized.
Also late in July 2025, the United States and South Korea reached a framework agreement, finalized in October 2025. The threatened 25 percent US Liberation Day tariffs on Korea were capped at 15 percent, but other tariffs remained in place. Korea agreed to invest $350 billion in approved US projects. Threatened tariffs on imports from Korea amounted to $20.3 billion annualized.
Negotiating leverage with Canada remains a continuing saga. On an annualized basis, threatened US tariffs amount to $1.3 billion.
Industrial subsidies
The Global Trade Alert recently uncovered a fresh avenue for tariff reversals: reduce or eliminate tariffs on imports by US firms that make approved commitments to invest in US plants. Between April and August 2026, executive orders authorized the secretary of commerce to negotiate company-specific tariffs to address what the Trump administration identified as national security threats under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. The administration imposed or threatened new duties on pharmaceuticals, aluminum, polysilicon derivatives, and drones. The government struck agreements with several companies under this authority but has not disclosed the terms. US imports of the specified items amounted to $264 billion in 2025. Threatened tariffs on aluminum, before the reversals, amounted to roughly $5.8 billion annualized.
Consumer prices
After more than five years of high inflation, Americans are sensitive to any policy that stretches household budgets. Serious research shows that tariffs are almost entirely paid by US households and business firms, not by foreign exporters.
Trump's executive order issued November 14, 2025, exempted from all Liberation Day tariffs a range of tropical products plus beef, oranges, and tomatoes. The order did not mention consumer price

articles.title: White House Reports Progress in India-U.S. Trade Talks as Piyush Goyal Says Agreement Nears Completion - INDIA New England News
articles.summary: White House Reports Progress in India-U.S. Trade Talks as Piyush Goyal Says Agreement Nears Completion  INDIA New England News
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON– The White House has described ongoing trade negotiations with India as productive, signaling progress toward a bilateral agreement as Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said the two countries had completed most of their discussions and were working to finalize the remaining details.
The Trump administration said negotiations were continuing as Washington and New Delhi sought to conclude a trade agreement aimed at strengthening economic ties between the two countries.
“Representatives of the Trump administration continue to engage in productive talks with Indian officials to secure a historic trade deal that puts Americans and America First,” White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said.
Middleton also emphasized the relationship between President Donald Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, suggesting that both leaders remained committed to expanding cooperation.
“President Trump and Prime Minister Modi have a close personal relationship, and both leaders remain committed to lifting bilateral ties to new levels,” Middleton said.
The White House comments followed remarks by Goyal at the India-Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague on Monday, where he indicated that negotiations had entered their final stages.
“We have concluded most of the discussions and are fine-tuning the agreement,” Goyal said.
Goyal is visiting Germany and the Netherlands with an Indian business delegation as part of efforts to strengthen commercial relationships with European partners.
During his remarks, he also highlighted India’s expanding international trade relationships, noting that the country had concluded nine free trade agreements over the past four and a half years.
India and the United States announced a framework for the first phase of a bilateral trade agreement in February, marking an important step toward resolving longstanding trade disputes.
Under the framework announced February 7, Washington reduced tariffs on Indian goods to 18% from 50%.
However, subsequent changes in U.S. tariff policy, including developments following a Supreme Court ruling on tariffs, prompted additional negotiations between the two countries.
Trade officials from Washington and New Delhi have held several rounds of discussions in recent weeks to resolve outstanding issues.
Goyal met U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministerial meeting in Milwaukee on October 1.
The discussions continued when an Indian delegation led by Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal visited Washington for meetings with U.S. officials from October 15 to 17.
The progress was also acknowledged by Secretary of State Marco Rubio during his visit to Mumbai on October 20.
Speaking to reporters, Rubio indicated that the two countries were approaching an agreement, with only a limited number of unresolved issues remaining.
“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without (inaudible) agreement. I think there’s a small number of items to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly,” Rubio said.
Rubio clarified that while the State Department does not directly negotiate trade agreements, it remains closely involved in broader diplomatic discussions surrounding the negotiations.
“Obviously the State Department doesn’t negotiate trade agreements, but we are very much involved in what’s happening,” he said.
The negotiations have attracted considerable attention from businesses and policymakers in both countries because of their potential impact on tariffs, exports and investment.
Washington has been pressing India to increase purchases of American energy and technology products, while Indian exporters have sought greater access to the U.S. market and relief from tariffs.
As part of its broader trade commitments, India has expressed its intention to purchase $500 billion worth of American products over five years.
The proposed purchases include energy products, aircraft and aircraft components, precious metals, technology products and coking coal.
The commitments could substantially expand commercial ties between the two countries and provide opportunities for American manufacturers and exporters.
The United States remains India’s largest trading partner, making the outcome of the negotiations particularly significant for businesses on both sides.
Although neither government has announced a final agreement or a signing date, the latest statements from the White House and Indian officials indicate that negotiations have advanced considerably, with both sides focused on resolving the remaining differences. (Source: IANS)

articles.summary: Global firms look to India for growth as semiconductor expansion and trade gains beckon  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
The Hague [Netherlands], October 27 (ANI): Global companies see India's expanding manufacturing base and improving trade opportunities as drivers of business growth, with semiconductor maker Nexperia planning to double its revenue in the country over the next few years and DEPT expecting the proposed India-UK free trade agreement to ease business operations.
Speaking to ANI during Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal's visit to the Netherlands, Nexperia Interim CEO Stefan Tilgner said the company had signed a joint agreement with Tata to work on semiconductor development and manufacturing, while committing to triple its existing footprint in India within the next five years.
"We expect our company to double our revenue in India basically in the next few years and we have also commitments in place to actually triple our current existing footprint in the coming five years," Tilgner said.
He said India's economic growth, particularly in the automotive sector, presented significant opportunities for Nexperia. Automotive accounts for more than half of the company's total business, while energy infrastructure, data centres and other applications could offer additional avenues for expansion.
Tilgner also highlighted the government's semiconductor strategy, support for manufacturing investment and the emergence of raw material suppliers as factors relevant to the sector. He said India's talent pool was another advantage at a time when skilled talent was becoming scarce in several other countries.
"We see certainly that the announced semiconductor strategy 2.0 is very important for us as a semiconductor company," he said.
Separately, Dimi Albers, Global CEO of DEPT, said the proposed India-UK free trade agreement could help businesses grow by making interactions across supply chains easier and reducing regulatory barriers.
"I think we are all here to grow our business and this allows us to do that better, right?" Albers said, adding that easier movement of people and products would support business expansion.
Albers, who met Goyal, described the interaction as valuable for companies looking to expand their presence in India. He said the discussion brought together businesses interested in contributing to their own growth as well as the Indian economy.
Together, the remarks highlight how India's manufacturing growth and prospects for easier cross-border trade could create new opportunities for global businesses. (ANI)

articles.full_text:
India's growth seen losing momentum after strong start to fiscal year: Poll
The US-Israeli-led war with Iran has so far had limited impact on economic growth, but it has pushed up inflation mainly through higher energy costs
Listen to This Article
Economic growth in India is forecast to have slowed this fiscal year from a surprisingly strong pace and hover around 7% over the forecast horizon as higher energy costs add to near-term inflation risks, a Reuters poll of economists found.
The US-Israeli-led war with Iran has so far had limited impact on economic growth, but it has pushed up inflation mainly through higher energy costs. The Reserve Bank of India has raised rates once and is expected to do so twice more, to 6.0%, by end-March.
But with no planned major policy changes, Asia's third-largest economy is forecast to carry on growing steadily at a rate most forecasters agree will not bring about any significant improvements in job prospects, particularly for young people.
"7% growth is quite healthy, especially in this climate. But is that healthy for India? I would say it's probably just average," said Miguel Chanco, chief emerging Asia economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics.
Gross domestic product was forecast to grow 7.1% in the fiscal year ending March 2027, according to the median estimate in an October 19-26 Reuters poll, down from 7.7% in FY 2025-26. Growth was then expected to ease to 7.0% in FY 2027-28.
Also Read
The forecast for this fiscal year was in line with RBI expectations as well as an earlier Reuters survey and broadly matched that of the International Monetary Fund.
Economists have underestimated India's growth in 10 of the past 12 quarters despite forecasts generally clustering within a narrow range close to 7%.
JOBS OUTLOOK DIMS AS OIL, AI WEIGH
Private investment, a key driver of job creation, expanded by nearly 12% in the June quarter. Forecasters say sustaining such growth will become increasingly difficult if oil prices remain elevated. Crude oil futures are trading around $116 a barrel, about 60% above pre-war levels.
India has also missed out on the surge in AI investment that has lifted growth in other Asian economies like South Korea.
"India's caught between its own ... domestic issues of low, insufficient private investment growth, but also there's this global backdrop of AI making it unnecessary to hire as many entry-level positions," said Chanco. "It's causing a lot of dissatisfaction among the youth in India, and rightly so."
A student-led movement that began as online satire has spilled onto India's streets in recent months, reflecting growing concerns over education and jobs despite the country's rapid economic growth.
Inflation is squeezing household budgets as savings dwindle. Price growth was forecast to average 6.1% this quarter and remain above the RBI's 4% medium-term target at least until end-2027.
That outlook is slightly higher than the forecast in last month's survey.
"Stronger cost pass-through (from higher energy prices) and gradually rising services inflation increase the risk that elevated price pressures become embedded," wrote Kunal Kundu, India economist at Societe Generale.
Households are at risk from future cuts to welfare spending, which has long helped support demand and protect millions from poverty, economists say. The 2026-27 budget projected a 4.5% cut in food, fertiliser and petroleum subsidies.
"The fact not only the central government but state governments are also actually providing significant amounts of cash to protect consumption, which is basically all the schemes they are running, immediately tells me all is not well," said Indranil Pan, chief economist at Yes Bank.

articles.title: India threatens a key UK trade deal benefit by seeking 150% duties on bulk Scotch - Vinetur

articles.full_text:
An industry group warned that customs officials could nullify the 75% tariff cut for major whisky importers
Tuesday, October 27, 2026
India’s attempt to deny lower tariffs to some bulk Scotch whisky imports is threatening a key part of the trade agreement it signed with the United Kingdom, according to a letter from an Indian industry group reported by Reuters.
The dispute centers on how Indian customs authorities classify bulk Scotch concentrates imported by major spirits companies, including Diageo and Pernod Ricard. If those products are excluded from the tariff cuts agreed under the UK-India trade deal, importers could face the full 150% duty instead of the reduced 75% rate that took effect in July.
Reuters reported that the International Spirits and Wines Association of India, or ISWAI, wrote to India’s commerce minister to warn that the customs issue “risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the UK.” The group said the “preferential tariff treatment negotiated … could effectively become unavailable for these imports,” according to the report.
The trade agreement between India and the UK came into force in July. Under its terms, India cut import duties on UK whisky from 150% to 75%, with a further reduction to 40% scheduled over the next 10 years. That tariff relief was seen as a major concession in a market that has long been difficult for foreign spirits producers because of high import taxes.
The current dispute appears to focus not on bottled Scotch sold directly to consumers, but on concentrated or bulk Scotch shipped to India for local processing, blending, or bottling. According to Reuters, Indian investigators have privately told companies that those bulk Scotch concentrates do not qualify for the reduced tariff under the trade deal. Instead, authorities say the imports must be declared under a customs category that still carries the full 150% duty.
That interpretation would raise costs for companies that rely on bulk imports as part of their India operations. It would also weaken one of the practical commercial benefits promised by the trade pact, particularly for large multinational distillers with established bottling and distribution businesses in the country.
Earlier this month, India’s Directorate of Revenue Intelligence, or DRI, visited premises linked to Pernod Ricard and to Diageo’s Indian subsidiary as part of the classification inquiry, according to the information cited by Reuters. Allied Blenders & Distillers, a local spirits company, also said last week that tax officials had visited in connection with the import of bulk Scotch into India.
The visits suggest the matter has moved beyond a technical interpretation issue and into an active enforcement stage. Companies now face the possibility that past or current imports could be examined under a stricter classification standard, with direct consequences for duties owed.
The dispute comes at a sensitive time for the broader UK-India commercial relationship. The tariff cut on whisky was one of the most closely watched parts of the bilateral trade deal because it addressed a long-standing complaint from British exporters and Scotch producers. India is one of the world’s largest whisky markets by volume, but high duties have historically limited access for imported premium spirits.
For producers such as Diageo and Pernod Ricard, the classification question matters both because of immediate cost exposure and because India is a strategic growth market. Importing Scotch in bulk can be an important part of managing pricing, supply chains, and local production economics. If those imports are denied the lower tariff, companies could see a sharp increase in landed costs and a narrower benefit from the agreement than they expected when the deal took effect.
ISWAI’s intervention shows concern within the industry that the issue could spread beyond a single customs dispute. The group’s reported warning suggests companies fear that a restrictive interpretation by Indian authorities could, in practice, block the tariff concession for a category of imports that many major players use.
The UK government has said it is engaging with India on the matter. In a statement cited in the report, Britain’s Department for Business and Trade said: “We are working with the government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal.”
That response indicates the issue has become a government-to-government concern, not just a private dispute between importers and customs officials. The question now is whether the two sides can align on how the agreement applies to bulk Scotch products, or whether companies will remain exposed to the higher tariff while the matter is reviewed.
Neither the reported letter nor the comments cited by Reuters indicate that the underlying trade agreement itself is being formally reopened. The immediate issue is how Indian authorities are applying customs classifications under the current regime. But for the companies involved, the effect could be similar to losing a negotiated trade benefit if bulk imports are treated as ineligible.
The investigation also highlights the importance of technical customs definitions in trade deals. Even where governments agree to lower headline tariff rates, the commercial value of that commitment can depend on how specific products are classified at the border. In this case, the difference between treatment at 75% and treatment at 150% is large enough to affect pricing, margins, and import strategy for some of the world’s biggest spirits groups.
Reuters reported that it had seen the ISWAI letter. The news agency said the industry group’s members include Diageo and Pernod Ricard. Requests for comment from ISWAI and India’s commerce ministry were not immediately detailed beyond that reporting. The issue remains under scrutiny as companies, industry bodies, and officials assess whether bulk Scotch imports will receive the same tariff relief that the UK and India agreed to put in place from July.

Pune: BE Hub Udaan, the first accelerator cohort from BE Hub, an initiative by the founders of Saturo Technologies, has opened applications for its 12-week startup acceleration programme aimed at early-stage deep-tech and technology-led businesses.
Applications open on October 27, 2026, and will close on November 18, 2026.
The programme is scheduled to begin on November 23, 2026, with only five to six startups set to be selected for the inaugural cohort.
Under the theme Build. Accelerate. Rise., BE Hub Udaan aims to support ambitious founders in validating their ideas, strengthening their business models, accessing relevant industry networks and preparing their ventures for growth.
The accelerator is designed for founders building deep-tech startups and scalable technology-led businesses.
Eligible sectors include semiconductor technologies, electronics, advanced materials, scientific innovation, engineering, software-as-a-service (SaaS), artificial intelligence (AI), enterprise technology, automation, fintech infrastructure and other technology-enabled solutions.
The programme is looking for founders with a clearly defined problem, a credible solution and the commitment to turn their ideas into sustainable businesses.
BE Hub Udaan to Offer Mentorship and Business-Building Support
Through BE Hub Udaan, selected startups will receive structured mentorship, business model validation support, go-to-market guidance, founder development opportunities and access to industry professionals and the wider startup ecosystem.
The 12-week accelerator will focus on helping founders strengthen their understanding of customer needs, refine their value propositions, evaluate pricing and revenue models, and assess the commercial viability of their solutions.
The programme will also support startups in developing customer acquisition strategies, distribution channels, partnerships and early revenue opportunities.
- Structured Mentorship
Selected founders will receive guidance from entrepreneurs, industry professionals and domain experts relevant to their business challenges.
The mentorship is intended to help founders address specific business and execution priorities as they develop their ventures.
- Business Model Validation
The accelerator will help founders work on customer problems, value propositions, pricing strategies, revenue models and the commercial viability of their solutions.
- Go-to-Market and Growth Support
BE Hub Udaan will support participating startups in developing clearer approaches to customer acquisition, distribution, partnerships and early revenue generation.
- Industry and Ecosystem Access
Founders will have opportunities to connect with relevant experts, potential partners, prospective customers and members of the startup ecosystem, subject to availability.
- Founder Development
The programme will focus on strengthening entrepreneurial decision-making, execution discipline and the ability to build and lead teams.
- Investor Readiness
Participating founders will receive support in improving their pitches, financial understanding, business narratives and preparation for future fundraising conversations.
- Potential Seed Investment
A select number of startups participating in BE Hub Udaan may be considered for seed investment by BE Hub or relevant investment partners.
However, investment consideration will be separate from admission to the accelerator. Any investment will be subject to evaluation, due diligence, necessary approvals and mutually agreed terms. Joining the programme does not guarantee funding.
BE Hub Udaan Programme Structure and Timeline
The BE Hub Udaan accelerator will run for 12 weeks, beginning on November 23, 2026. The programme will be organised into four stages, covering startup validation, product and business development, execution and growth, and preparation for the next phase.
- Stage 1: Discover and Validate
The first stage will focus on clarifying the customer problem, identifying the target market, refining the value proposition and determining the assumptions that need to be tested.
- Stage 2: Build and Strengthen
During this stage, founders will work on improving their products, prototypes or minimum viable products (MVPs), strengthening their business models and developing processes to gather and incorporate customer feedback.
- Stage 3: Execute and Grow
The third stage will focus on go-to-market strategy, acquiring early customers, developing partnerships, generating revenue and identifying key operational priorities.
- Stage 4: Prepare for the Next Stage
The final stage will involve reviewing progress, defining future milestones and preparing for potential partnerships, fundraising discussions or investment evaluation.
The detailed session calendar and milestone expectations will be shared with the startups selected for the first BE Hub Udaan cohort.
Eligibility Criteria for BE Hub Udaan
BE Hub Udaan is open to early-stage founders and founding teams building deep-tech or technology-led startups. Applicants should have a clearly defined customer or industry problem, demonstrate commitment to building their venture and show the potential to develop a sustainable and scalable business.
Applicants should also be willing to participate in programme activities, mentorship sessions and progress reviews.
Startups may apply at different stages of development, including the idea stage, provided they have a credible development plan. Ventures with prototypes, MVPs or operating products are also eligible to apply.
Student founders and first-time entrepreneurs are welcome to apply if they can demonstrate commitment, capability and a credible plan for developing their businesses.
The programme is open to a broad range of technology-led ventures, including those working in SaaS, AI, machine learning (ML), cloud technology, fintech infrastructure, B2B platforms, semiconductors, electronics, advanced materials, enterprise technology and automation.
Final selection will depend on the startup’s fit with the programme, founder commitment, business potential and alignment with the focus of the cohort.
Any consideration for seed investment will involve a separate assessment and due diligence process. Selection for the accelerator will not automatically qualify a startup for investment.
BE Hub Udaan: Application Dates and Key Details
- Applications open: October 27, 2026
- Application deadline: November 18, 2026
- Programme start date: November 23, 2026
- Programme duration: 12 weeks
- Number of startups selected: Five to six
- Participation fee: No participation fee for the accelerator programme
- Eligible startups: Early-stage deep-tech and technology-led ventures
- Potential investment: Select startups may be considered separately for seed investment
There is no participation fee for the accelerator programme. Any separate commercial arrangement, if applicable, will be communicated transparently in advance.
BE Hub has also clarified that no equity is automatically taken simply because a startup joins the accelerator. Any investment arrangement will be documented separately under mutually agreed terms.
