articles.title: India-US Trade Deal: Where the Edge Lies, and What It Will Cost - orfonline.org
articles.summary: India-US Trade Deal: Where the Edge Lies, and What It Will Cost  orfonline.org
articles.full_text:
A bilateral trade agreement could give India an edge over its competitors in select sectors of the US market, but it must be negotiated with the country’s wider partnerships in mind
Image Source:  Getty Images 
The India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) has been under negotiation since early 2025, but is yet to be ratified. India’s objective is to secure the BTA to gain a competitive advantage over its peers in the US market, which would enable it to boost export revenue, employment, and economic growth.
The US already accounts for around 20 percent of India’s merchandise exports, but export growth has remained subdued amid tariff uncertainty. India’s trade patterns with the US (Figure 1) show that merchandise exports to the US have levelled off since 2024-25, while imports from the US have kept rising, shrinking India’s trade surplus. A durable BTA with preferential market access can provide greater certainty, allowing India to convert its existing presence in the US into sustained export growth.
The significance of the US market extends beyond export revenue, as its demand also supports substantial employment across India’s key export sectors. Textiles employ over 45 million people, while footwear and leather, and electronics, support a further 4.5 million and 2.5 million jobs, respectively. India, however, competes with Vietnam, Indonesia, Bangladesh, and Japan for the same market across its key export sectors (Figure 1). The question, therefore, is where the BTA can give India an edge, and whether these gains can be secured without incurring wider strategic costs in its relations with partner countries.
Figure 1: India-US Merchandise Trade and Export Composition
Source: Authors’ own using TradeStat and IBEF
To identify where the BTA can give India an edge over its competitors, the first step is to assess the overlap between India’s export basket and theirs in the US market. This overlap is measured using the Export Similarity Index (ESI), which captures how closely India’s export structure resembles that of a competitor. Decomposing the index by sector then shows which sectors drive the overlap, indicating where a BTA-led advantage could be explored.
Vietnam and Indonesia show the highest overlap with India, both at approximately 73 percent, driven by Electrical Machinery, Equipment & Electronics. Japan’s similarity stands at close to 50 percent, anchored by Engineering Goods, while Bangladesh diverges from India chiefly because of its concentration in Textiles.
Figure 2: Export Similarity Index 2021–2025
Source: Authors’ own using UN Comtrade, Finger & Kreinin (1979) and Federal Reserve Note.[1]
India’s electronics competitiveness in the US hinges on market access relative to Vietnam and Indonesia. India faces a general 10 percent Section 301 tariff rate (aimed at addressing unfair trade practices), the same as Indonesia but lower than Vietnam’s 12.5 percent. The sharper differentiator is supply-chain scrutiny: Vietnam and Indonesia are flagged as major transshipment hubs for electronics and machinery. An estimated US$67 billion in China-linked goods was transshipped through Mexico, India, and Vietnam in 2025, resulting in a US$28 billion loss in US tariff revenue. While India is named among these transit routes, it is not singled out as an electronics transshipment hub. Thus, if India can position itself as a trusted supply-chain partner through robust rules of origin and customs enforcement, it can gain an edge through the BTA.
India’s engineering exports compete primarily with Japan. Both countries face a 50 percent Section 232 tariff (addressing national security concerns surrounding steel, aluminium, and copper), but Japan receives an exemption on certain steel derivatives, which puts it at an advantage. Japan’s higher net Section 301 rate of 12.5 percent offers India some room, but Japan’s deeper strategic relationship with the US and its existing 2020 trade agreement give it an institutional advantage beyond tariffs. India’s scope to gain a decisive edge through the BTA is, therefore, limited here.
If India can position itself as a trusted supply-chain partner through robust rules of origin and customs enforcement, it can gain an edge through the BTA.
India’s textile challenge from Bangladesh lies less in export similarity and more in market access. Both face a 10 percent Section 301 rate, but Bangladesh has a zero-tariff pathway for certain apparel using US-origin inputs, as well as a dedicated textile Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) under Section 301, an allocation it shares with Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia. The advantage, however, has yet to translate into stronger performance: Bangladesh’s ready-made garment exports to the US fell in FY2025-26, losing share to Vietnam and Cambodia. A favourably designed BTA can put India in a competitive position to fill this emerging market gap.
The remaining sectors present a mixed picture. Pharmaceuticals give India its strongest advantage, as it faces limited competition from other economies. Chemicals, however, offer a weaker competitive case, with no sector-specific concession for India or its competitors. In footwear and leather, India has an edge over Vietnam under Section 301 but lacks a comparable advantage over Indonesia, which faces the same 10 percent rate.
The BTA’s value cannot be reduced to a single tariff number. While the negotiations should assess sectoral strengths, their terms remain shaped by broader issues, such as India’s sensitivity around agriculture and dairy, US demands for greater market access, and the dispute over Russian oil purchases. Such factors temper the agreement’s scope and pace, irrespective of India’s competitive advantages.
These differences illustrate why the BTA’s value cannot be reduced to a single tariff number. While the negotiations should assess sectoral strengths, their terms remain shaped by broader issues, such as India’s sensitivity around agriculture and dairy, US demands for greater market access, and the dispute over Russian oil purchases. Such factors temper the agreement’s scope and pace, irrespective of India’s competitive advantages.
The competitive gains carry implications beyond tariffs. The US agreements with Cambodia and Malaysia show that tariffs alone do not determine whether a deal is struck. Under their terms, Washington could terminate the agreements if the partner entered into an arrangement with a third country that was deemed to jeopardise US interests. After the US Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariffs in early 2026, Malaysia’s trade minister declared the agreement “null and void”. For India, such provisions would need to be considered carefully. India has strong trade and strategic partnerships with countries that compete in the US market, so conditions that create diplomatic sensitivities or affect broader market access must be negotiated with these wider relationships in mind. India’s ongoing dialogue with the US underscores these trade-offs, with talks now at a “plateau”, held up by differences over agriculture, dairy, and Russian oil.
The success of the BTA will ultimately hinge on striking a balance between leveraging preferential market access to build sustainable export competitiveness, maintaining the breadth of India’s international trade relationships, and safeguarding sensitive domestic sectors.
The BTA should be viewed as more than a vehicle for securing preferential tariffs. Its value lies in addressing the sector-specific constraints that shape India’s competitiveness, but the gains need to be weighed against their wider diplomatic costs. India should prioritise opportunities where the economic benefits outweigh the strategic trade-offs, while safeguarding its existing partnerships. The success of the BTA will ultimately hinge on striking a balance between leveraging preferential market access to build sustainable export competitiveness, maintaining the breadth of India’s international trade relationships, and safeguarding sensitive domestic sectors.
Arya Roy Bardhan is a Junior Fellow with the Centre for New Economic Diplomacy at the Observer Research Foundation.
Damayantee Majumdar is a Research Intern at the Observer Research Foundation.
[1] ESI is calculated across six broad sectors mapped from HS 2-digit codes using export mirror data (US imports). The sectoral aggregation follows prior ESI studies (e.g., composite ESI analysis of China’s exports, REICE 2020). The index ranges from 0 (completely dissimilar export profiles) to 100 (when export profiles are identical), capturing how closely the sectoral composition of exported goods between both countries coincides.

articles.title: Chile trade deal nearing conclusion; Canada negotiations gaining pace: Piyush Goyal - India's News.Net

The Hague [Netherlands], October 27 (ANI): India's trade negotiations with Chile are nearing conclusion, while discussions with Canada are making good progress, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said, signalling the government's push to expand the country's trade partnerships and open up new markets for Indian goods and services.
Speaking at a press conference during his Netherlands visit on Monday, Goyal said negotiations with several trading partners were progressing, with Mexico also keen on an early-harvest arrangement, while talks with the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) had recently begun.
"I can see Chile is quite ripe for conclusion, Canada is making very good progress," Goyal said, outlining the status of India's ongoing trade negotiations.
He said discussions with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) could take longer due to the West Asia crisis, although India was ready to accelerate the process. The proposed trade agreement with the Eurasian region was still being assessed, as it covers goods but excludes services, he added.
Goyal said India was pursuing trade agreements to improve market access for domestic businesses and create opportunities across sectors, including textiles, leather, footwear, agriculture, marine products, auto components and precision engineering.
He said labour-intensive industries could benefit from lower duties under trade agreements, while improved access for agricultural and marine products could increase demand for goods produced by farmers and fishing communities. Micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) making auto components and precision engineering products could also see opportunities for employment generation.
The minister said India was also likely to see large-scale investments in modern technologies in the coming years, as international businesses explore opportunities in the country.
On global capability centres (GCCs), Goyal said companies were increasingly considering shifting work to India instead of relocating Indian talent abroad. He said this could reduce costs for businesses while increasing India's foreign exchange earnings, tax revenues and domestic consumption.
Goyal also said the government had strengthened its approach to trade negotiations through greater stakeholder consultations and standard operating procedures to preserve institutional knowledge and ensure that domestic sensitivities were protected.
He said India would expand international exhibitions and business delegations to help Indian companies explore overseas markets and familiarise foreign businesses with investment opportunities in the country. (ANI)

articles.title: US, Brazil and Israel elections put India’s trade worth billions in focus - The Economic Times
articles.summary: US, Brazil and Israel elections put India’s trade worth billions in focus  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The priorities, however, are varied. India and the US are close to finalising a trade pact, Brazil is emerging as an increasingly important commercial partner, and negotiations for a free trade agreement with Israel are underway. Political changes in any of these countries could influence how quickly those plans move forward.
US: Trade pact in focus ahead of midterms
Americans head to the polls on November 3 for the midterm elections, with control of both chambers of Congress at stake. Republicans are looking to hold on to their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, while Democrats are hoping to make gains.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Democrats leading Republicans 47% to 36% among registered voters on the generic congressional ballot. A loss of either chamber would make it harder for President Donald Trump to push through his agenda during the remaining two years of his term.
For India, the timing is significant. New Delhi and Washington are in the final stages of discussions over a proposed trade agreement, with both sides trying to settle outstanding issues.
The proposed pact is particularly important for Indian exporters in sectors such as textiles, leather, engineering goods and pharmaceuticals, where tariff concessions could improve access to the American market.
Much, however, will depend on the final terms of the agreement and when it comes into effect.
The midterm results may not directly determine the fate of the negotiations, but a change in the balance of power in Congress could complicate Trump's broader trade agenda. That makes the political developments in Washington worth watching for New Delhi.
Brazil: Trade ambitions gain momentum
India's relationship with Brazil has grown steadily over the years, moving beyond conventional trade into a wider partnership covering energy, agriculture, technology and diplomacy.
Brazil is already India's largest trading partner in Latin America and the Caribbean. And the numbers suggest there is room for further growth.
Bilateral trade reached $15.21 billion in 2025, an increase of more than 25% from $12.2 billion the previous year, according to the Ministry of External Affairs. The momentum continued into 2026, with trade touching $8.77 billion in the first six months, nearly 37% higher than in the corresponding period last year.
Also Read: India’s ‘dear friend’ is back in power in Brazil, and a $30 billion trade opportunity is on the table
India exported goods worth $8.35 billion to Brazil in 2025, led by petroleum products, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and engineering goods. Imports, valued at $6.85 billion, included crude oil, soybean oil, raw sugar, cotton and iron ore.
Both governments now want to take the relationship further.
During his visit to India in February 2026, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva proposed raising bilateral trade to $30 billion, going beyond the $20 billion target for 2030 that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had earlier announced.
The two countries also share common interests in groupings such as BRICS and the India-Brazil-South Africa Dialogue Forum, where they have often called for a greater voice for developing economies.
Lula has also suggested exploring the use of the Indian rupee and Brazilian real for bilateral trade settlements, although he has acknowledged that such a shift would not be easy.
On the commercial front, India and Brazil already have a framework for tariff concessions through the India-Mercosur Preferential Trade Agreement. Expanding that arrangement could open up more opportunities for exporters and investors.
The political direction Brazil takes after its election will therefore be important for India, particularly as the two countries look to turn ambitious trade targets into actual business.
Israel: Proposed FTA could expand market access
India's ties with Israel have traditionally been driven by defence cooperation, but the relationship has widened considerably in recent years. Trade, technology, agriculture and innovation are now increasingly important parts of the partnership.
During Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Israel in February 2026, the two countries elevated their relationship to a Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity.
The October 27 election in Israel comes against this backdrop, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political future in focus.
For New Delhi, the immediate concern is less about the electoral contest itself and more about what follows, particularly the continuity of defence projects, technology partnerships and ongoing trade negotiations.
Also Read: Israel votes today: What’s at stake for India as Bibi faces tough fight
India and Israel are currently negotiating a free trade agreement covering goods, services, rules of origin, intellectual property and customs procedures. If concluded, the deal could make it easier for businesses on both sides to access each other's markets.
Bilateral merchandise trade stood at $3.93 billion in FY26. India's exports to Israel include engineering goods, chemicals, textiles and machinery, while imports largely comprise chemicals, machinery, electronics and other industrial products.
The two countries have also established a bilateral investment agreement aimed at giving investors greater protection and certainty.
But trade is only one part of the relationship.
Israel remains an important defence and technology partner for India, with cooperation spanning defence platforms, joint manufacturing, research and development, and technology transfers. Both sides have also agreed to work more closely in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and semiconductors.
Agriculture, water management and space technology are other areas where the two countries see opportunities to expand cooperation.
A change in government could bring fresh priorities in some of these areas. For India, the challenge will be to keep negotiations moving and maintain the momentum of existing partnerships, irrespective of the election outcome.
What the elections mean for India
The three elections present different questions for New Delhi.
In Washington, attention is on whether the political balance after the midterms could affect Trump's trade agenda as India and the US work towards an agreement. In Brazil, the focus is on sustaining a growing economic relationship and pushing bilateral trade towards the ambitious targets set by both governments. In Israel, continuity in defence cooperation and progress on the proposed FTA will remain important.

Lula’s re-election in Brazil could strengthen India ties in trade, rare earths, energy, defence and Global South cooperation.
New Delhi: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election is expected to provide continuity to India-Brazil relations, creating opportunities for deeper economic cooperation, access to critical minerals and stronger coordination on global issues. Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated Lula on his victory on October 26, 2026, and expressed his desire to strengthen the strategic partnership between the two countries. ￼
The election outcome comes at a time when India is looking to expand its economic engagement with Latin America, diversify supply chains and strengthen cooperation with emerging economies. Brazil, one of the region’s largest economies, has become an important partner for New Delhi in areas ranging from trade and energy to technology, defence and international diplomacy.
Lula’s continued leadership could help maintain momentum in these efforts, particularly as India and Brazil seek to increase bilateral trade and develop alternative sources of critical minerals needed for industrial growth and the energy transition.
PM Modi congratulates Lula on re-election
Modi welcomed Lula’s victory in Brazil’s presidential run-off election and said India looked forward to working closely with Brazil on shared priorities, including the interests of the Global South and the development of a more inclusive international order.
The Indian prime minister said both countries would continue to strengthen cooperation across several sectors while advancing a shared vision of a more equitable and sustainable world. The message highlighted the importance New Delhi attaches to its relationship with Brasília.
Lula also welcomed the election result, saying that the Brazilian people had made history through their participation in the democratic process. His victory over right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro will allow him to begin another non-consecutive presidential term, extending his role in Brazilian and regional politics.
For India, the result offers continuity in its engagement with a leader who has supported closer cooperation among developing countries and greater representation for emerging economies in international institutions. ￼
Trade target of $30 billion by 2030
Trade is expected to remain one of the central pillars of India-Brazil relations. During Lula’s recent engagement with India, both countries agreed to work towards increasing bilateral trade to $30 billion by 2030.
The target reflects efforts to build on the expansion of commercial ties and identify new opportunities for businesses in both countries. According to the Hindustan Times report, bilateral trade increased by 25% in 2025 compared with the previous year.
India is seeking to broaden its economic partnerships beyond traditional markets, while Brazil offers opportunities across agriculture, mining, energy, manufacturing and other sectors. Stronger trade links could help Indian businesses gain greater access to Latin American markets and enable Brazilian companies to expand their presence in India.
The two governments have also discussed expanding the India-MERCOSUR trade agreement. MERCOSUR is a South American regional economic bloc, and a broader trade arrangement could provide a framework for improving commercial access and supporting business engagement.
Achieving the $30 billion target, however, will depend on sustained business participation, investment, trade facilitation and the ability of both governments to address practical barriers to commerce. ￼
Rare earths and critical minerals gain importance
One of the most significant areas of cooperation is the supply of rare earth elements and other critical minerals. These materials are essential for several modern industries, including electric vehicles, renewable energy technologies, electronics and advanced manufacturing.
India’s growing industrial requirements have increased the importance of securing reliable supplies of these resources. Diversifying mineral imports is also relevant to the country’s efforts to reduce excessive dependence on concentrated global supply chains.
Brazil is considered an important potential partner because of its substantial mineral resources. The two countries have concluded agreements covering rare earths and mining, creating a basis for closer collaboration in mineral exploration, production and supply chains. ￼
For India, cooperation with Brazil could support long-term requirements associated with infrastructure development, clean energy and advanced manufacturing. Access to dependable mineral supplies could become particularly important as industries expand production of technologies that depend on specialised materials.
However, mineral agreements do not automatically guarantee immediate supplies. Their impact will depend on investment, extraction capacity, processing infrastructure, environmental standards and the commercial arrangements established by companies in both countries.
Brazil could also benefit from Indian participation in mineral-related industries, technology partnerships and manufacturing. The relationship therefore offers opportunities for cooperation across different stages of the supply chain rather than being limited to the exchange of raw materials.
Energy, technology and defence cooperation
India and Brazil have also identified energy and technology as important areas for expanding their strategic partnership.
Energy cooperation includes conventional hydrocarbons as well as renewable energy, ethanol blending and sustainable aviation fuel. Brazil’s experience with biofuels could complement India’s efforts to diversify energy sources and develop cleaner alternatives for transport and industry.
Both countries are also exploring cooperation in technology and innovation, including artificial intelligence, semiconductors, supercomputing and digital public infrastructure. These sectors have growing importance as governments seek to modernise public services, strengthen digital economies and improve technological capabilities.
India’s experience in digital public infrastructure could offer opportunities for collaboration with Brazil, while Brazilian participation could create new avenues for Indian technology companies and research institutions.
Defence is another area of interest. Brazil could benefit from India’s experience in defence manufacturing, space technology and digitalisation, while stronger industrial engagement could create opportunities for collaboration between companies and institutions.
The success of these initiatives will depend on converting political commitments into practical projects, investment and sustained cooperation between businesses and government agencies. ￼
India and Brazil share priorities at BRICS and G20
Beyond economic ties, India and Brazil have worked together through multilateral platforms, including BRICS and the Group of Twenty (G20).
Both countries have supported reforms to international institutions and called for greater representation of developing economies in global decision-making. Their cooperation is particularly relevant to discussions on global governance, climate change, development financing and the role of emerging markets.
The Global South broadly refers to developing countries whose interests often include fairer access to finance, technology and international decision-making. India and Brazil have sought to strengthen their collective influence on these issues.
Brazil’s diplomatic engagement has also been relevant to India’s efforts to build consensus within BRICS. The Hindustan Times report noted Brazil’s role in helping secure a unanimous joint declaration at the recent BRICS Summit despite differences between Iran and the United Arab Emirates.
Lula’s re-election could help maintain this cooperation, although the positions of individual countries may continue to differ on security, trade and other international questions. ￼
US tariffs and the changing global trade environment
The India-Brazil partnership has gained additional significance amid trade tensions with the United States.
According to the Hindustan Times report, the US imposed 50% tariffs on both India and Brazil in 2025, although the reasons cited by Washington differed for the two countries. The measures encouraged New Delhi and Brasília to discuss closer economic cooperation and ways to address the impact on their economies.
Lula reached out to Modi during that period, and both leaders emphasised the importance of cooperation in trade, energy, defence and technology. Their discussions reflected a shared interest in maintaining economic relationships while defending their respective national interests.
For India, stronger links with Brazil could contribute to market diversification and reduce dependence on a limited number of trading partners. For Brazil, closer ties with India could provide additional commercial opportunities in Asia.
This does not mean either country will move away from its existing relationships with major global powers. Both governments will continue to balance their economic and diplomatic interests while negotiating with partners such as the United States and China.
Instead, closer India-Brazil engagement could provide both countries with more options as they navigate changes in international trade and competition for strategic resources. ￼

Lula’s re-election provides an opportunity for India and Brazil to build on existing agreements rather than start their bilateral engagement afresh. L&T Tech Services bags five-year Nokia contract to support R&D in India
The partnership will establish a dedicated offshore development centre in India, with work spanning 5G networks, AI-driven operations, software development and next-generation telecom infrastructure
Listen to This Article
L&T Technology Services (LTTS) has signed a five-year contract with Nokia to support the Finnish telecom equipment maker’s engineering and research and development activities in India, the company said in an exchange filing on Monday.
Under the agreement, LTTS will back Nokia R&D programmes in product engineering, software development, system integration and product support. It will set up a dedicated Offshore Development Center (ODC) in India for the work, and create a separate engineering team to support Nokia’s Technology Center globally.
The partnership comes as Nokia steps up its R&D efforts around AI infrastructure and advanced connectivity technologies. LTTS said the new centre would combine data-centre-grade computing and AI infrastructure engineering with the development of next-generation telecom solutions.
The Indian engineering team will work across areas including 5G networks, intelligent automation, AI-driven operations and AI infrastructure, collaborating with Nokia’s global R&D teams through an integrated operating model.
For LTTS, the deal aligns with its Lakshya 31 strategy, particularly its focus on next-generation computing and AI infrastructure. The company sees these capabilities as increasingly important to the evolution of future communication networks and intelligent data centres, according to the statement. 
Also Read 
“India is an important innovation hub for Nokia, and LTTS is a critical partner that will bring engineering expertise and mechanisms that will help us expand our R&D footprint and accelerate innovation,” Vivek Jaiswal, senior vice-president of engineering at Nokia, said.
Alind Saxena, executive director and president–strategic initiatives and growth markets at LTTS, said the agreement reflected the confidence global technology companies placed in the company’s engineering expertise.
LTTS, a subsidiary of Larsen & Toubro, provides engineering research and development services across sectors including telecommunications, industrial products, medical devices and transportation. As of September 30, 2026, the company had 24,035 employees, 21 global design centres, 31 global sales offices and 111 innovation labs, according to its release.
The companies did not disclose the financial value of the five-year contract.

India-Russia Ties Beyond Trade: How History, Defence and Strategic Trust Shape a Lasting Partnership
From Soviet-era industrial assistance and diplomatic support during the 1971 war to defence cooperation, cultural exchanges and energy trade after 2022, India-Russia relations have endured shifting geopolitical realities. As bilateral trade expands, both countries face the challenge of reducing trade imbalances, diversifying economic cooperation and preserving strategic autonomy in an increasingly multipolar world.
"We cannot be friends with anyone at the expense of our friendship with India." This remark by Russian President Vladimir Putin reflects the foundational spirit of India-Russia relations—a bilateral bond that cannot be evaluated through the narrow metrics of commercial trade balances, defense procurement contracts, or transactional agreements alone. Prime Minister Narendra Modi similarly characterized the partnership between New Delhi and Moscow as extending beyond the official interactions of incumbent governments or political leaderships, describing it as an enduring friendship rooted in the hearts of their respective peoples. Modi's observation that even a young child in India regards Russia as a trusted friend captures the deep historical reservoir of popular goodwill that remains the partnership's greatest institutional asset. President Putin likewise emphasized the unbroken continuity of this bilateral alignment across shifting geopolitical currents. In modern international relations, such declarations are frequently dismissed as diplomatic rhetoric; in the case of India and Russia, however, they rest upon more than six decades of shared diplomatic history during which both nations maintained their strategic alignment despite ideological realignments, armed conflicts, international sanctions, domestic economic restructuring, and changes in government.
In contemporary international statecraft, the notion of permanent interstate friendship is viewed with widespread skepticism, often summarized by the maxim that sovereign states have neither permanent friends nor permanent enemies, but only permanent interests. There is clear analytical truth in this principle: no sovereign nation can guide its foreign policy over the long term on sentimental attachment alone. Yet it is equally true that enduring strategic partnerships are not governed entirely by short-term balance-sheet calculations. Over time, shared historical memories, proven reliability during national crises, deep institutional ties, and cultural exchanges construct layers of institutional trust that resist sudden geopolitical fractures. The relationship between India and Russia exemplifies this characteristic. Over the decades, their bilateral trade volumes remained modest, defense procurement experienced technical friction, shifting international pressures tested their diplomatic alignments, and their domestic economic priorities diverged. Despite these pressures, the core foundation of the partnership endured. Evaluating India-Russia relations through trade figures alone obscures the historical depth and strategic resilience of the relationship.
Curiosity regarding Russia and the Soviet Union existed within Indian political and intellectual circles long before the achievement of formal independence in 1947. The 1917 Russian Revolution had a major impact upon anti-colonial struggles and socialist political thought across the colonized world, leading numerous architects of the Indian national movement to examine the economic transformations unfolding in early Soviet society. Jawaharlal Nehru took a sustained intellectual interest in the Soviet developmental model: visiting the Soviet Union in 1927, he wrote extensively on its rapid industrialization and social policies, approaching the Soviet experiment as a nationalist leader exploring pathways for post-colonial economic development. While Nehru disagreed with aspects of the Soviet political system, he was drawn to its centralized planning, public-sector investments, and state-led heavy industrialization. Following Indian independence, these early intellectual connections evolved into the foundation for long-term strategic and economic cooperation.
India and the Soviet Union established formal diplomatic relations in April 1947, months before India achieved sovereign independence from the British Empire. In the years following 1947, bilateral ties expanded without being structured into a formal military alliance. The guiding principle of Nehru’s foreign policy was non-alignment: independent India declined to join either the American- or Soviet-led ideological blocs of the Cold War. Non-alignment, however, did not mean maintaining an artificial, equidistance from the two superpowers; rather, India sought external developmental and security partnerships based on its national interests. The Soviet Union began providing financial and technical assistance to build India's public sector and heavy industrial base. Industrial landmarks such as the Bhilai Steel Plant became symbols of this economic cooperation, followed by Soviet technical participation in power generation, machine tool manufacturing, petroleum exploration, scientific research, and higher technical education.
The Soviet Crucible: Heavy Industry, Defense Architecture, and 1971
The state visit of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru to the Soviet Union in 1955, followed that same year by the reciprocal tour of Soviet leaders Nikita Khrushchev and Nikolai Bulganin across India, elevated the bilateral relationship to a new diplomatic tier. This was a formative period during which an independent India was assembling its domestic industrial infrastructure, requiring external technology and capital to develop heavy industry and technical expertise. While developmental assistance was available from Western capitals, it often arrived with conditionalities and political alignments that conflicted with India’s independent, non-aligned foreign policy. The Soviet Union offered an alternative model of industrial collaboration, engineering training, and defense transfers that accommodated India's state-led mixed economy. Over time, this economic engagement built widespread public trust within India: Soviet universities, research laboratories, and manufacturing institutes became vital centers for training generations of Indian engineers, technical specialists, defense personnel, and scientists.
Defense cooperation deepened this strategic interdependence. During its early post-independence decades, India required modern fighter aircraft, main battle tanks, naval combatants, and submarines to build its defense capabilities. The Soviet Union emerged as India’s primary external defense supplier. The historic agreements governing the licensed manufacture of MiG-21 interceptors involved both military procurement and the transfer of technical expertise for domestic assembly within India. Over the following decades, the frontline inventories of the Indian Air Force, Army, and Navy were built largely upon Soviet and Russian platforms. The strategic significance of this defense relationship was immense: military hardware is not a transactional commodity, as operational platforms require lifelong supply chains for ammunition, spare parts, component overhauls, mid-life upgrades, and logistical support during wartime. Once a sovereign military integrates its doctrine and maintenance around a specific defense technology, an enduring strategic interdependence develops that shapes bilateral ties for decades.
The decisive historical test of Indo-Soviet ties arrived during the crisis of 1971. The brutal military crackdown in East Pakistan, paired with the mass exodus of millions of refugees into eastern India, placed immense humanitarian, economic, and security burdens upon New Delhi. Confronted with a regional security crisis and complex international alignments, India signed the historic Treaty of Peace, Friendship, and Cooperation with the Soviet Union in August 1971. This treaty marked a turning point in Indian foreign policy, providing New Delhi with strategic deterrence against external intervention by rival major powers. During the Indo-Pakistani War of December 1971, the Soviet Union repeatedly utilized its veto power in the United Nations Security Council to block resolutions demanding an immediate, unconditional ceasefire that would have halted Indian operations before the liberation of Bangladesh was achieved. This diplomatic support in the Security Council gave the Indian political and military leadership the operational time required to achieve their objectives.
During that same conflict, the United States dispatched the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Enterprise and Task Force 74 of the Seventh Fleet into the Bay of Bengal, an event that left an enduring mark on Indian strategic thinking. Concurrently, Soviet naval deployments in the Indian Ocean provided strategic deterrence, though popular assertions that a single Soviet naval detachment directly turned back the American fleet simplify the complex naval maneuvering of the period. Nevertheless, Soviet diplomatic, intelligence, and military backing in 1971 proved critical to India’s security objectives. The birth of an independent Bangladesh, the victory of the Indian armed forces, and Moscow's firm support cemented the Soviet Union's standing in Indian public consciousness as an indispensable and reliable strategic partner. This shared historical experience built a foundation of popular goodwill toward Moscow that persisted across subsequent generations.
